sources.locator: train.csv, test.csv and test_labels.csv of the Toxic Comment Classification Challenge (dataset card: CC0, comment text CC BY-SA 3.0)
prepare.py (competition test set with released labels) and grade.py (mean column-wise ROC AUC, rows marked -1 dropped)
competition definition (task, labels, metric)

notes: Data: the competition files from a Hugging Face mirror (thesofakillers, revision 50f3c926; CC0 per the card, which restates the competition data page; comment text from Wikipedia under CC BY-SA 3.0), fetched and hash-locked by scripts/prepare_kaggle.py. Verified identical to the data MLE-bench uses: MLE-bench's prepare.py (openai/mle-bench 507f92e1, unchanged) run on the mirror reproduces the MD5 checksums MLE-bench records for all four files it prepares from Kaggle's download (public train.csv, test.csv, sample_submission.csv, private test.csv). Counts: 159,571 training comments (positives: toxic 15,294, severe_toxic 1,595, obscene 8,449, threat 478, insult 7,877, identity_hate 1,405), 153,164 test comments, of which 63,978 carry labels and 89,186 are marked -1 (all six labels together).

Split and metric follow MLE-bench: train on the competition training file, score the labelled competition test rows with sklearn's roc_auc_score(average='macro') over the six labels as in its grade.py; on the seed's predictions MLE-bench's grade.py (with the -1 rows included in the answers, as MLE-bench stores them) returns exactly the evaluator's value. Deviation: the candidate receives only the 63,978 scored test comments; MLE-bench hands over all 153,164 (the unscored ones only deter hand labelling), so they are not available as unlabelled text here. Every candidate is scored on these test labels and that score is the search signal (the evaluator holds back no validation split), so scores reached by search are selected on the test set; the paper says only that EurekAgent's agents receive official scores from a hidden grading service, not what that service computed during its MLE-Bench runs.

The score covers all scored test rows, i.e. Kaggle's public and private leaderboard rows together (as in MLE-bench); Kaggle leaderboard values and medal thresholds come from the private rows only and are not directly comparable.

Compute: fit_predict runs on CPU with 4 threads in a sandboxed child process (no network, no GPU, no pretrained weights or embeddings, no external data, 3.5 GB memory) and is killed 15 s after a 600 s wall-clock budget. MLE-bench agents had a GPU, 24 hours and internet access to pretrained models, which the strongest solutions of this competition used; scores here measure what can be trained from scratch in 10 CPU-minutes. The budget is wall-clock time, so scores depend on the machine's speed and load.

Label isolation: held-out labels live in data/kaggle/jigsaw/private and the raw download cache; the child receives only public file paths, and on macOS sandbox-exec denies it reading those directories (an audit hook in the child adds the same restriction at the Python level elsewhere). Residual risk: the shared evaluator template imports the candidate module once in the evaluator process before scoring, so module-level code runs unsandboxed there.
Seed (word TF-IDF and one logistic regression per label) scores 0.9753 in 9-12 s of fit_predict on an Apple M4 Max shared with other jobs.
superseded_limitations: Task appears in the paper MLE evaluation but no corresponding dataset wrapper, run config or evaluator package is present in the pinned public EurekAgent repository.

sources.locator: NoisyOffice (Espana-Boquera, Pastor-Pellicer, Castro-Bleda, Zamora-Martinez; CC BY 4.0): SimulatedNoisyOffice noisy and clean grey-level images
prepare.py (ground truth = clean grey level / 255) and grade.py (RMSE over all pixels)
competition definition; its acknowledgement names the NoisyOffice authors and the UCI repository

notes: Analogue built from the UCI NoisyOffice corpus (CC BY 4.0), not from Kaggle's files. The competition credits the NoisyOffice authors and UCI for its data, and the simulated part matches it in count and size (216 noisy grey-level images of 540 x 258 or 540 x 420 pixels; Kaggle had 144 training and 72 test images), but pixel identity with Kaggle's files was not checked (no Kaggle access).

Each NoisyOffice partition (TR, VA, TE) is one text passage typeset in 18 fonts, and every typeset page appears with 4 noise types (folded, wrinkled, coffee stains, footprints). Split by text: the 144 noisy images of the TR and VA passages (with their clean pages) are the training set and the 72 noisy images of the TE passage the test set. MLE-bench instead re-splits Kaggle's 144 training images at random 80/20 (random_state 0), which puts other noise versions of the same typeset page into training; the text-disjoint split here is harder, so scores are not comparable with MLE-bench or Kaggle values and medal thresholds do not apply. Every candidate is scored on this test set and that score is the search signal (the evaluator holds back no validation split); LoongFlow's released MLE-bench evaluator (agents/ml_agent/examples/mlebench/eval_program.py at 945c78bc) instead scores candidates on their out-of-fold predictions for the training data and grades the test submission only in a debug mode. The paper states no budget, hardware or split for its MLE-bench runs.

Images are handed over as uint8 arrays (the noisy files are RGB PNGs with three identical channels and are reduced to one channel exactly); presentation order is seeded and carries no font, noise or passage information. Metric: RMSE over every pixel of every test image against the clean grey level / 255, pooled over images as in MLE-bench's grade.py; predictions are not clipped.

Compute: fit_predict runs on CPU with 4 threads in a sandboxed child process (no network, no GPU, no pretrained weights, 3.5 GB memory) and is killed 15 s after a 300 s wall-clock budget; models are trained from scratch. The budget is wall-clock time, so scores depend on the machine's speed and load.

Label isolation as in the other kaggle tasks: clean test pages are in data/kaggle/noisyoffice/private, which the child cannot read (sandbox-exec on macOS, audit hook elsewhere); the candidate module is still imported once, unsandboxed, by the shared evaluator template.
Seed (lookup table from noisy grey level to mean clean intensity) scores 0.0903 RMSE in under a second.

sources.locator: PatchCamelyon valid and test files: images, labels and slide metadata (data CC0 per github.com/basveeling/pcam; MIT per the Zenodo record)
README: labels refer to the central 32 x 32 pixel region; splits are slide-disjoint; data licence
grade.py (ROC AUC; utils.prepare_for_auroc_metric requires probabilities in [0, 1])
competition definition: PCam without duplicate patches

notes: Analogue built from PatchCamelyon (PCam), labelled as such: the Kaggle competition uses PCam without its duplicate patches and otherwise keeps PCam's data and splits (competition data page), but its files are not used here. Data: PCam's 'valid' and 'test' files from Zenodo record 2546921 (the GitHub README swaps the two names; the MD5s agree), 65,536 RGB patches of 96 x 96 pixels from 183 Camelyon16 whole-slide images (54 Camelyon16 training slides, 129 test slides); labels equal the metadata's center_tumor_patch flag for every patch. PCam's 6 GB training file is not used.

Preparation: 8,045 exact duplicate patches (identical pixels; no label conflicts) are removed, leaving 57,491; each patch is cut to its central 48 x 48 pixels (the labelled central 32 x 32 region plus an 8-pixel margin) to keep CPU training feasible, while the competition provides the full 96 x 96 patches.

Split by whole-slide image: slides are drawn in a seeded order (numpy RandomState(0) permutation of the sorted slide names) into the test set until it holds at least 20% of the patches: 39 slides with 11,672 test patches (40.1% positive) and 144 slides with 45,819 training patches (43.7% positive). MLE-bench re-splits Kaggle's training images at random (test ratio about 0.21, no slide grouping), so patches of one slide appear on both sides there; the training set here is also about a fifth of Kaggle's. Scores are not comparable with Kaggle or MLE-bench values, and medal thresholds do not apply. Every candidate is scored on these test labels and that score is the search signal (the evaluator holds back no validation split); LoongFlow's released MLE-bench evaluator (agents/ml_agent/examples/mlebench/eval_program.py at 945c78bc) instead scores candidates on their out-of-fold predictions for the training data and grades the test submission only in a debug mode, and EurekAgent's paper does not say what its hidden grading service returned during its MLE-Bench runs.

Metric: ROC AUC of the predicted probabilities (sklearn roc_auc_score as in MLE-bench's grade.py; predictions outside [0, 1] are invalid as in MLE-bench's prepare_for_auroc_metric); on the seed's predictions MLE-bench's grade.py returns exactly the evaluator's value.

Compute: fit_predict runs on CPU with 4 threads in a sandboxed child process (no network, no GPU, no pretrained weights, 3.5 GB memory) and is killed 15 s after a 600 s wall-clock budget; scores depend on the machine's speed and load. A small three-block CNN trained for 480 s on a shared Apple M-series machine reached ROC AUC 0.865 (probe, not part of the task). EurekAgent ran each MLE-Bench Lite competition once with 24 hours and one GPU (its Section 4.3) and its agents had web access; LoongFlow states no budget or hardware for its MLE-bench runs.

Label isolation: test labels are in data/kaggle/pcam/private and the raw downloads in .cache/kaggle-raw, which the child cannot read (sandbox-exec on macOS, audit hook elsewhere); the candidate module is imported once, unsandboxed, by the shared evaluator template.
Seed (logistic regression on colour statistics of the crop and its centre) scores ROC AUC 0.8046 in about 6 s.

sources.locator: NMD-18 (CC0): 3,000 sesquioxides with DFT-relaxed geometries, formation energy per atom and band gap
Sutton et al. 2019: competition dataset, Vegard's-law input geometries, relaxed-geometry comparison (Table 2)
grade.py (mean of the RMSLEs of formation_energy_ev_natom and bandgap_energy_ev)
competition definition

notes: Analogue with relaxed input geometries. Data: ColabFit's NMD-18 (CC0), the 3,000 materials of the competition (2,400 training and 600 test materials) with their DFT targets. Its geometries are the DFT-relaxed structures: all 3,000 are identical (cell, species order and positions to 1e-5 Angstrom) to nmd18r.xyz of the curated NMD-18 release on qmml.org, and only 5 have a cell within 1e-3 Angstrom of nmd18u.xyz, which that release's readme names as the competition dataset (Vegard's-law geometries). nmd18u reproduces the competition's training and test tables (cell lengths, angles, cation fractions, space groups) to their 4-decimal rounding for all 3,000 materials, checked against the competition tables in the authors' GitHub repository csutton7/nomad_2018_kaggle_dataset (MLE-bench's prepare.py run on its train.csv reproduces the MD5 checksums MLE-bench records for its prepared train.csv, test.csv and answers, so these are the competition tables). qmml.org and that repository state no licence and were used only for these checks.

The competition gave Vegard's-law starting structures as inputs while its targets belong to the relaxed structures; here the relaxed structures are the inputs. This makes the task easier: on the same materials and split, the seed model scores 0.0655 with the relaxed inputs and 0.0772 with the competition's Vegard's-law geometries (Sutton et al. 2019 report that switching the top three competition models to relaxed geometries changes their test MAEs by 1-2 meV/cation for formation energy and 1-14 meV for band gap). Scores are therefore not comparable with Kaggle or MLE-bench values, and medal thresholds do not apply. The table columns (cation fractions, cell lengths and angles) are recomputed from the relaxed cells with the code that reproduces the competition tables from the Vegard's-law cells; relaxed cell lengths differ from the competition's by 0.10 Angstrom on average.

Targets in competition units: ColabFit stores formation energy per atom; the competition's formation_energy_ev_natom is 5/2 of it (per cation of the M2O3 cell), which reproduces the competition's training and test values for all 3,000 materials to 6e-17 eV; band gaps are identical.

Split: ColabFit does not keep the competition ids or order, so MLE-bench's split (90/10 of the 2,400 competition training materials, random_state 0) cannot be replayed; a seeded 90/10 split of all 3,000 materials (ordered by ColabFit configuration id, numpy RandomState(0) permutation) gives 2,700 training and 300 test materials, re-numbered from 1 as MLE-bench does. Every candidate is scored on these 300 test materials and that score is the search signal (the evaluator holds back no validation split); LoongFlow's released MLE-bench evaluator (agents/ml_agent/examples/mlebench/eval_program.py at 945c78bc) instead scores candidates on their out-of-fold predictions for the training data and grades the test submission only in a debug mode. The paper states no budget, hardware or split for its MLE-bench runs.

Metric: mean over the two targets of scikit-learn's root_mean_squared_log_error, as in MLE-bench's grade.py; a prediction scikit-learn rejects (<= -1 in the installed version 1.9) makes the candidate invalid.

Compute: CPU, 4 threads, sandboxed child process without network or pretrained models, 3.5 GB, killed 15 s after a 300 s budget. Label isolation as in the other kaggle tasks (sandbox-exec on macOS, audit hook elsewhere; the candidate module is imported once, unsandboxed, by the shared evaluator template). The budget is wall-clock time, so scores depend on the machine's speed and load.
Seed (gradient-boosted trees on the table columns, volume per atom and the space group) scores 0.0655 in about 4 s.

sources.locator: Kaggle_RYOS_trainset.csv (MIT): the SN_filter = 1 rows of the competition's train.json
Wayment-Steele et al. 2022, Deep learning models for predicting RNA degradation via dual crowdsourcing
prepare.py (240 SN_filter > 0 test rows, random_state 0) and grade.py (MCRMSE over reactivity, deg_Mg_pH10, deg_Mg_50C on scored positions)
competition definition

notes: Data: Kaggle_RYOS_trainset.csv of eternagame/KaggleOpenVaccine (commit b95af835, MIT), the 1,589 rows of the competition's train.json with SN_filter = 1, in their original order with the original row index (0 to 2399) and the competition's columns; its extra columns derived from labels or models (k_deg, half-life, model predictions) are dropped.

Split replayed from MLE-bench: the test set is the 240 rows that MLE-bench's prepare.py samples among the SN_filter > 0 rows (pandas sample, n = 240, random_state 0). Running MLE-bench's prepare.py unchanged on a 2,400-row train.json made of the public rows at their original index plus placeholders for the 811 missing rows selects the same 240 RNAs and reproduces, byte for byte, the MD5 checksums MLE-bench records for its answers file (private test.csv: ids and all five targets at 107 positions) and its sample submission. Its prepared test.json (inputs) is not reproduced under any column order or column subset, so some input strings (sequence, structure, loop type) or their serialization may differ from Kaggle's train.json; this was not resolved (no Kaggle access). Deviation: the training set is the remaining 1,349 SN_filter = 1 rows; MLE-bench's training set also contains the 811 low signal-to-noise rows (SN_filter = 0) of train.json, which the public file omits (2,160 rows in total). Every candidate is scored on these 240 test RNAs and that score is the search signal (the evaluator holds back no validation split); LoongFlow's released MLE-bench evaluator (agents/ml_agent/examples/mlebench/eval_program.py at 945c78bc) instead scores candidates on their out-of-fold predictions for the training data and grades the test submission only in a debug mode. The paper states no budget, hardware or split for its MLE-bench runs.

Metric exactly as MLE-bench's grade.py: MCRMSE, the mean over reactivity, deg_Mg_pH10 and deg_Mg_50C of the RMSE pooled over the first seq_scored = 68 positions of all test RNAs (config.yaml names a log-loss grader, but grade.py computes MCRMSE). The candidate returns only the scored array (240, 68, 3) instead of the 107-position five-column submission; the unscored columns and positions carry no weight in either.
The test RNAs come from the competition's training sequences (as in MLE-bench), not from the 130-nt private test constructs, so Kaggle leaderboard values and medal thresholds are not comparable.

Compute: CPU, 4 threads, sandboxed child process without network, external folding packages or pretrained models (structure and predicted_loop_type columns are given), 3.5 GB, killed 15 s after a 300 s budget. Label isolation as in the other kaggle tasks (sandbox-exec on macOS, audit hook elsewhere; the candidate module is imported once, unsandboxed, by the shared evaluator template). The budget is wall-clock time, so scores depend on the machine's speed and load.
Seed (mean target per nucleotide and loop type) scores 0.4237 MCRMSE in under a second.

sources.locator: copy of Google's Patent Phrase Similarity dataset (train, validation and test splits)
original release, CC BY 4.0
Aslanyan and Wetherbee 2022: 48,548 pairs, 973 anchors, anchor-disjoint 75/5/20 split
grade.py (Pearson correlation)
competition definition

notes: Data: Google's Patent Phrase Similarity dataset (CC BY 4.0, the data of the competition per its data page) from the Hugging Face copy tasksource/patent-phrase-similarity (revision ff186879). Checked: 36,473 / 2,843 / 9,232 pairs in the train / validation / test splits (48,548 in total, as in the dataset paper), 733 / 57 / 183 anchors with no anchor shared between splits, 106 CPC contexts. The competition's training file has 36,473 rows like the training split; row-level identity was not checked (no Kaggle access).

Split: the dataset's own anchor-disjoint split; the candidate trains on the training and validation splits (39,316 pairs) and is scored on the test split (9,232 pairs, unseen anchors). MLE-bench instead re-splits the competition's training file at random 90/10 (random_state 0), which shares anchors between training and test and is easier; the copy has no competition ids, so that split cannot be replayed. Scores are therefore not comparable with MLE-bench or Kaggle values, and medal thresholds do not apply. The fine-grained rating column of the dataset is not given (the competition provides only the score). Every candidate is scored on the 9,232 test pairs and that score is the search signal (the evaluator holds back no validation split); LoongFlow's released MLE-bench evaluator (agents/ml_agent/examples/mlebench/eval_program.py at 945c78bc) instead scores candidates on their out-of-fold predictions for the training data and grades the test submission only in a debug mode. The paper states no budget, hardware or split for its MLE-bench runs.
Metric: Pearson correlation of predicted and annotated scores (scipy.stats.pearsonr, as in MLE-bench's grade.py); constant predictions are invalid.

Compute: CPU, 4 threads, sandboxed child process without network, pretrained language models, word vectors or CPC title tables (the strongest competition solutions fine-tuned pretrained transformers), 3.5 GB, killed 15 s after a 300 s budget; models are built from the training pairs only. Label isolation as in the other kaggle tasks (sandbox-exec on macOS, audit hook elsewhere; the candidate module is imported once, unsandboxed, by the shared evaluator template). The budget is wall-clock time, so scores depend on the machine's speed and load.
Seed (cosine similarity of character 2-4-gram TF-IDF vectors, no training) scores Pearson 0.4496 in about 1 s.
